units.oneLiner: Keep every key in the slot array itself and, when the home slot is taken, probe the next slot and the next: the probes stay inside the cache line the first one fetched, Knuth's 1963 formulas say exactly what each load factor costs, and the price is clustering, which is why the table resizes before it is full and why the hash must scatter neighbors.
units.description: Linear probing on 65,536 slots against Knuth's 1963 formulas (within 1% to load 0.7) and a Python set over 1,200,000 operations: at load 0.9 a hit costs 5.315 probes but 1.540 cache lines against 2.570 and 2.570 for double hashing; clusters of 715 slots; tombstones 5.864 probes per miss against 1.698 for backward shift; a weak hash costs 1,056 probes per hit.
units.time: O(1) expected; (1 + 1/(1 - a)) / 2 probes per hit

units.plan_row: Open addressing × Linear probing. units.oneLiner: Keep one running level and move it a fraction alpha toward each observation: the forecast is the level, and the recursion is a weighted average of the whole past with weights alpha (1 - alpha)^k that fade geometrically, sum to one, and sit (1 - alpha)/alpha values back on average; fit alpha by squared one-step error and it lands on the Kalman gain.
units.description: Exponential smoothing: the recursion equals the unrolled geometric sum to 3e-14; the fitted alpha 0.390 +- 0.003 lands on the Kalman gain 0.390 over 150 series; one-step RMSE 1.284 against a floor of 1.281, moving average 1.321, naive 1.499, mean 4.662; a trend lags by b/alpha (0.96); a season trails by a month, 7.86 against 2.84.

units.oneLiner: Sort the jobs longest first and hand each to the machine that is least loaded so far: the long jobs settle while the machines are empty and the short ones level the ends, so the makespan is never worse than 4/3 - 1/(3m) times the optimum (Graham 1969, tight), against 2 - 1/m for the same rule in arrival order; one sort, one pass, and a lower bound as the receipt.
units.description: Graham's LPT rule against exact optima on 300 random instances: 1.0212 × OPT mean, 1.1739 worst, inside 4/3 − 1/(3m); arrival order 1.1221 and 1.4688; the tight families hit 7/6, 11/9, 15/12, 19/15 and 2 − 1/m exactly; MULTIFIT wins 148, ties 100, loses 52; LPT met the lower bound on 20 of 20 thousand-job instances.
units.time: O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n log m) placements
units.space: O(m) machine loads plus the sorted order
units.plan_row: Job scheduling approximation × Longest processing time. Puzzle 209, optimization-or (problemSlug shop-scheduling, the atlas problem page carrying "Makespan approximation"; sibling live lessons first-fit-decreasing-descending-size-order (131), branchbound-fractional (5), work-stealing-random-victims (114)). Solution job_scheduling_approximation_longest_processing_time.py (0.2 s, prints OK): list scheduling to the least loaded machine, the LPT wrapper, the lower bound max(p, ceil(sum/m)), branch and bound on jobs sorted longest first (one machine tried per distinct load, pruned by the remaining work and by min load + next job), brute force over all m^n assignments, first fit decreasing with a capacity search (MULTIFIT), a move-or-swap local search from the LPT schedule, and the two tight-family generators. ORACLES: (1) exact solver equals brute force on 60 instances of 4 to 8 jobs on 2 or 3 machines; (2) 300 random instances (n = 10..14, m = 2..4, sizes 1..50): LPT/OPT mean 1.0212, worst 1.1739, optimal on 75 of 300, worst by machine count 1.0526 / 1.1111 / 1.1739 against the bounds 1.1667 / 1.2222 / 1.2500; arrival order mean 1.1221, worst 1.4688 (bound 2 - 1/m); MULTIFIT mean 1.0099, worst 1.0833, against LPT wins 148, ties 100, losses 52; local search from LPT mean 1.0045, worst 1.0566, never above LPT; exact search 310 nodes mean, lower bound equal to OPT on 240 of 300; (3) tight families: LPT returns 4m - 1 against OPT 3m, 7/6, 11/9, 15/12, 19/15 for m = 2 to 5 (4/3 - 1/(3m) exactly); the arrival-order family (m(m-1) unit jobs then one job of length m) returns 2m - 1 against m, LPT optimal there; (4) 20 instances of n = 1,000 on m = 10 (sizes 1..100): LPT met the lower bound on 20 of 20, MULTIFIT never below it, arrival order 0.87% above on average and 1.11% at most; (5) adversarial order at m = 10: list 19 against OPT 10 (ratio 1.90), LPT 10; (6) exact search at m = 3 with sizes 1..1000: 988 / 4,795 / 54,121 / 27,022 nodes at n = 12 / 16 / 20 / 24 (asserted more than tenfold growth). Two author corrections recorded in the header: the draft expected LPT about 10 percent above the optimum on small random instances (measured 2 percent), and expected MULTIFIT to tie LPT on most instances (it won about half). Figure: mean and worst ratios for four methods beside Gantt charts of the m = 3 tight family (LPT 11, optimum 9); cite Graham 1966 (DOI 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1966.tb01709.x), Graham 1969 (DOI 10.1137/0117039), Coffman, Garey, Johnson 1978 (DOI 10.1137/0207001), Hochbaum and Shmoys 1987. units.oneLiner: Stand at each node, check every pair of its neighbors for an edge, and divide the hits by three: the exact triangle count and every local clustering coefficient in one pass priced by the sum of degree choose two, so the hubs decide the bill and the degree-ordered forward algorithm, with every edge pointed uphill, is the escape when they do.
units.description: The node-iterator against four referees: brute force, trace(A^3)/6, and the forward algorithm agree on 40 small graphs and three families (94, 3,615, 205 triangles); ER mean 148.5 against C(n,3)p^3 = 143.8; six hubs take 43.4% of 23,282 pair checks where forward spends 6,550 steps (3.6x fewer); all 35,820,200 triples cost 1,539x.
units.time: O(sum of C(d, 2)) pair checks, the wedge count; forward O(m sqrt m)
units.space: O(n + m): a neighbor set per node
units.baseline: Forward algorithm (edges pointed uphill in degree)
units.plan_row: Triangle counting × Node-iterator. units.oneLiner: Project y onto the columns of X, but do it through the small ledger (X^T X) b = X^T y: one pass over the rows, a p by p Cholesky, the covariance for free, and 0.41x the flops of QR, at the price of seeing the condition number squared, which is harmless until it is not.
units.description: Least squares by the normal equations against Householder QR and the exact Gauss-Markov formulas: Cholesky equals QR to 1.8e-15 at 108,108 flops against 263,870; over 400 seeds the 95% intervals cover 0.951 and the variances match sigma^2 (X^T X)^-1; kappa(X^T X) = kappa(X)^2 on eight degrees until Cholesky fails at degree 12 where QR errs 6.4e-9.
units.time: O(n p^2) to form X^T X, O(p^3) to factor
units.space: the p x p ledger plus one row
units.baseline: Gradient descent on the same objective

units.oneLiner: Open the first center anywhere, then k minus one times open the next at the point farthest from every center so far: the farthest remaining point and the k centers are k + 1 points pairwise at least the radius apart, so any k centers must serve two of them from one place and the optimum is at least half the radius; a factor-two guarantee in k passes, the best any polynomial algorithm can promise.
units.description: Gonzalez's farthest-first traversal against exact optima on 230 small instances: 1.285 × OPT mean, 1.922 worst, optimal on 20, with r ≤ min witness distance ≤ 2 OPT on every one; exactly 2.000 on k far-apart copies of {0, 1, 2}; on 1,000 points with k = 10 a radius of 2.806 in 1.0 ms against k-means++ 4.185, Lloyd 3.507, PAM 4.478, random 5.546.
units.time: O(nk) distances: k passes over n points
units.space: O(n) for one distance per point

units.oneLiner: Flood a breadth-first wave from the source pin, labeling every cell it reaches with its distance, until the wave touches the target; then walk the labels back, D - 1, D - 2, down to zero, and the cells you stepped on are a shortest wire. Every label is exact, so the first touch is optimal and a dead wave is a proof that no path exists; the price is labeling most of the grid.

units.space: one label per labeled cell (12 bits on a 60 x 60 grid), 2 bits with Akers coding
units.baseline: Soukup's line probe with a wave fallback

Solution carry_lookahead_adder_generate_propagate_logic.py (8.1 s, prints OK): a netlist builder of two-input gates with balanced tree helpers, structural depth tracking (one unit per gate), and a bit-parallel evaluator that packs every test case into one big integer; six adders: ripple carry, flat single-level lookahead (explicit sums of products with literal and fan-in counts), hierarchical lookahead with four-column blocks built as a (G, P) tree then carries pushed top-down, Kogge-Stone and Brent-Kung prefix adders (carry-in folded into bit zero), and carry select with 4- or 8-bit blocks. ORACLES: (1) the (G, P) combining operator is associative on all 64 triples; (2) every adder equals Python integer addition bit for bit on all 512 four-bit and 131,072 eight-bit cases (both carry-ins) and on 6,009 random and crafted cases (all-ones chains, alternating patterns, top-bit collisions) at 16, 32, and 64 bits (the flat form to 16); (3) depth table (delays/gates): 4 bits ripple 9/20, lookahead 6/42, Kogge-Stone 7/29, Brent-Kung 8/26, carry-select 9/60; 8 bits 17/40, 11/87, 9/77, 12/59, 12/120; 16 bits 33/80, 13/190, 11/197, 16/128, 18/240; 32 bits 65/160, 19/383, 13/485, 20/269, 26/468; 64 bits 129/320, 21/782, 15/1,157, 24/554, 38/932 (8-bit blocks; 54 with 4-bit); asserted ripple = 2n + 1 at every width and (129, 21, 15, 24) at 64; (4) flat lookahead at 64 bits: the last carry's 64 generate terms hold 2,080 literals plus 65 in the carry-in term, fan-in 65 (asserted), all 64 carries without sharing 47,904 literals and 48,032 two-input gates; literals/fan-in by width 34/5, 164/9, 968/17, 6,544/33, 47,904/65; (5) gate ratios at 64 bits: hierarchical 2.44x ripple, Kogge-Stone 3.62x, Brent-Kung 1.73x; (6) Kogge-Stone without a carry-in measures 13 (asserted). Three author corrections recorded in the header: the draft's 12 to 14 delays for prefix adders measured 15 (Kogge-Stone) and 24 (Brent-Kung) with the carry-in folded in, 13 without; the hand estimates 22 and 16 for the block lookahead and Kogge-Stone measured 21 and 15; carry select with 4-bit blocks measured 54, so the page uses 8-bit blocks (38). Cards: self, Kogge-Stone adder × Parallel prefix carry (algoName), Parallel prefix sum × Blelloch scan (live lesson badge, puzzle 144), Wallace tree multiplier × Carry-save reduction (algoName). neverUse: the ripple adder or a flat lookahead at 64 bits (129 delays; fan-in 65 and 47,904 literals). Figure: critical path in gate delays against width for ripple, block lookahead, Kogge-Stone, Brent-Kung, and carry select on a log-width axis beside gate counts at 64 bits; cite Weinberger and Smith 1958 (NBS Circular 591), Kogge and Stone 1973 (DOI 10.1109/TC.1973.5009159), Brent and Kung 1982 (DOI 10.1109/TC.1982.1675982), Sklansky 1960. units.oneLiner: Mark each block's use set (variables read before any write) and def set (written before any read), start every IN and OUT empty with the exit's OUT fixed empty, and pop blocks off a worklist seeded in postorder: OUT is the union of the successors' IN, IN is use plus whatever in OUT the block does not define, and a predecessor is re-queued only when IN grew; union distributes over these transfer functions, so the fixpoint is exactly the set of variables some path ahead reads before writing, reached in about one and a half visits per block.

Puzzle 220, languages-compilers (problemSlug dataflow-analysis, the atlas problem page carrying "Dataflow analysis"; sibling live lessons reaching-definitions-forward-dataflow, puzzle 187, the forward twin, and register-allocation-graph-coloring, puzzle 162, the consumer). Solution live_variable_analysis_backward_dataflow.py (0.4 s, prints OK): a three-address IR over six variables with a seeded structured generator (if/else and while nested to depth 3, the entry reading every variable from input, the exit printing two), use/def per block with the branch condition as a final read, postorder by DFS, a worklist solver (predecessors requeued only when IN grew, asserting no set shrinks), a round-robin solver (one pass = the single-sweep negative example), two referees that never form a set equation (a per-variable reachability search; exhaustive simple-path enumeration), dead-store elimination checked by an interpreter (30 random inputs per program, loop visits capped identically), the interference graph with an exact backtracking chromatic number. MEASURED over 300 programs (8,497 blocks, 11,877 statements, 37,256 live facts, 217 with a loop): fixpoint equal to the reachability referee on 300 of 300 and to 114,559 enumerated simple paths on 300 of 300; postorder worklist 11,930 visits (1.40 per block) and 26,245 set ops; random worklist 25,872 (3.04) and 58,337; round robin postorder 28,815 (3.39) and 62,913 in 903 passes, max 5 = depth + 2, bound tight on 127 of 300; round robin reverse postorder (against the flow) 81,175 (9.55) and 177,775 in 2,156 passes; single sweep 8,497 visits, 5,287 live facts missing, its dead-store pass changed the output of 191 programs; 2,106 dead stores removed with identical output on 9,000 of 9,000 executions; interference graph 5.17 registers on average against 6 naive, chromatic number equal to the largest live set on 300 of 300. Author correction recorded: the draft expected the liveness graph to need about half the naive registers; measured 5.17 of 6 because every variable is read from input and printed late. Cards: self, Reaching definitions × Forward dataflow (live lesson 187), Register allocation × Graph coloring (live lesson 162), Dead code elimination × Mark-and-sweep on IR (all algoName pages present). neverUse: a single backward sweep that never revisits a block. Figure: a four-block loop solved backward where the head's read of y keeps the body's store live and one sweep would delete it, beside a bar chart of visits per block by schedule; cites Kildall 1973 (DOI 10.1145/512927.512945), Kennedy 1979, Chaitin 1982, Aho/Lam/Sethi/Ullman 9.2.5.
